summary: The note examines the growing global e-waste crisis driven by rapid gadget turnover, with only about 20% of e-waste recycled worldwide. It covers recycling complexity, health harms in places like Agbogbloshie, Ghana, and the roles of local programs, corporate responsibility and the right-to-repair movement. It also highlights education campaigns and AI-based recycling technology as part of the solution.
one_line: Overview of the global e-waste crisis, its health and environmental toll, and local, corporate, educational and technological responses.
key_facts: The Sustainable Electronics Initiative reported on October 12, 2023 that about 50 million tons of e-waste are generated worldwide each year, growing an estimated 3-5% annually.
Only about 20% of global e-waste is currently being recycled.
Dr. Helena Forsythe, an environmental scientist, calls e-waste an 'environmental time bomb' and says the average American replaced their smartphone every 18 to 24 months in 2023.
Dave Milligan, an environmental policy expert, says e-waste recycling is complex and not as straightforward as recycling paper or glass.
Modern electronics contain hazardous substances such as lead, mercury and cadmium, so dismantling them safely requires specialized facilities and skills.
On November 15, 2023, the Springfield city council launched an e-waste management program spearheaded by councilman Johnathan Park, focused on public education and accessible collection centers.
The Springfield program aims to ensure recovery of valuable materials like gold, silver and copper.

Consumer rights advocate Emily Tran argues manufacturers must make more sustainable, longer-lasting products, and that legislation is needed to counter planned obsolescence and restrictive repair policies.
Agbogbloshie, Ghana, is described as one of the world's largest e-waste dumping sites, where workers, often children, face respiratory and skin diseases, cancer and neurological damage.
Undocumented e-waste recycling operations with minimal regulatory oversight have also sprung up closer to home.
On September 20, 2023, the Sustainable Electronics Initiative launched the educational campaign 'Electronics: The Afterlife' with local school districts; campaign director is Marcus Yuen.
On December 1, 2023, NextGen Recycle announced an AI-powered sorting system meant to dramatically speed up recycling of electronic components.
